before:
We first examine the channel structure captured by the learned denoiser,
then evaluate its use in joint activity detection and channel estimation.
The receiver comparisons address estimation accuracy, pilot requirements,
access load, and transfer across channel profiles.
after:
We evaluate channel denoising, JADCE accuracy, pilot requirements,

before:
We consider the satellite uplink in Section~\ref{sec:system} with the
parameters in Table~\ref{tab:simulation-parameters}. Device locations
are sampled uniformly over the beam footprint. The propagation delays,
Doppler shifts, and array responses are determined by the same satellite
and device geometry. Large-scale propagation effects are compensated.
The channel follows the NTN-TDL-D power delay profile \cite{shen2025}, with the delay
spread drawn uniformly from $[30,50]$~ns. The line-of-sight component has
a uniformly distributed phase and fixed amplitude, while the diffuse
path gains are proper complex Gaussian. The path parameters remain fixed over each
transmission block. Unless otherwise stated, the access configuration uses
$K=40$, $Q=16$, and $p=0.1$.
after:
Table~\ref{tab:simulation-parameters} specifies the satellite uplink.
Devices are uniform over the beam footprint; delays, Doppler shifts,
and array responses share the same geometry. Large-scale propagation
effects are compensated. The NTN-TDL-D profile \cite{shen2025} uses
uniform delay spread $[30,50]$~ns, a line-of-sight gain of fixed
amplitude and uniform phase, and proper complex Gaussian diffuse gains.
Path parameters remain fixed per block. Defaults are $K=40$,
$Q=16$, and $p=0.1$.

before:
The training and validation sets contain $50{,}000$ and $5{,}000$
clean channel tensors of size $16\times16\times16$, respectively.
Four candidate channels are sampled from each physical scene before
activity masking, and the two sets use disjoint scenes. All channels
use the same fixed training normalization.
The channel denoiser uses Adam with a batch size of $64$, an
initial learning rate of $10^{-4}$, and an exponential moving average
with decay $0.999$. Training lasts $200$ epochs, with the checkpoint
selected by the minimum fixed-noise validation loss. The white-noise
reference uses the same channel bank and epoch budget.

observation-based noise estimates, with SNR defined by
\eqref{eq:snr}. STMP and GP-CCD-MP-DRE use activity threshold $0.5$, a minimum

The default new-message weights are $0.2$ and $0.4$, respectively.
Numerical derivative and stopping parameters are given in
Appendix~\ref{app:implementation}.

before:
We first evaluate the channel mean independently of activity detection
and receiver iterations, following the separate denoising evaluation
in \cite[Sec.~VI-B]{cai2026}. The direct observation is $R=H+W$ with
$\vect(W)\sim\CN(\mathbf0,v\I)$ and known $v$. The nominal denoising
SNR is $-10\log_{10}v$ in the fixed training coordinates. At each of
six SNR values from $-20$ to $30$~dB, we use $500$ physical scenes with
four channels per scene, giving $2{,}000$ channel samples. The two
neural estimators receive identical channels and noise realizations.
The labels AWGN and colored distinguish their training perturbations;
the test noise is white in both cases.

The reference estimators are least squares (LS), which returns $R$;
the Gaussian-prior estimate $P_{\rm tr}R/(P_{\rm tr}+v)$, where
$P_{\rm tr}$ is the mean element power of the normalized training
channels; and a genie-aided conditional MMSE reference. The genie is
given the true path geometry, path powers, and line-of-sight complex
gain, and its curve reports the analytic conditional MSE of the
remaining Gaussian path gains. The four sparse-recovery kernels are
also evaluated with an identity observation operator and known AWGN
variance, retaining their receiver settings and GNN weights;
GAMP-SBL retains its internal noise update.
after:
Following \cite[Sec.~VI-B]{cai2026}, we evaluate denoising separately
using $R=H+W$, $\vect(W)\sim\CN(\mathbf0,v\I)$, with known $v$
and nominal SNR $-10\log_{10}v$. Six SNRs span $-20$ to $30$~dB;
each uses $500$ scenes and four channels per scene ($2{,}000$ samples).
Both neural estimators receive identical channels and white test noise;
AWGN and colored label their training perturbations.

References are least squares (LS), returning $R$; the Gaussian-prior
estimate $P_{\rm tr}R/(P_{\rm tr}+v)$, where $P_{\rm tr}$ is the
normalized training-channel power; and genie-aided conditional MMSE.
Given true path geometry, powers, and line-of-sight gain, the genie
reports the analytic conditional MSE of the remaining Gaussian gains.
The four sparse-recovery kernels use an identity observation operator
and known AWGN variance, retaining their receiver settings and GNN
weights; GAMP-SBL retains its internal noise update.

before:
Figure~\ref{fig:cstmp-denoising} highlights the value of channel structure
beyond average coefficient power. The Gaussian-prior estimator rescales
all coefficients by a common factor, whereas the neural
estimators process the full channel tensor. At $0$~dB, the colored-trained
estimator attains $-17.98$~dB NMSE, compared with $-2.98$~dB for the
Gaussian-prior estimator. Both learned estimators also improve at high SNR,
while the sparse-recovery curves flatten under their adopted models and
settings. This behavior is consistent with residual approximation error
from the fixed dictionary and first-order offset model: reducing
observation noise alone does not remove these representation constraints.

The comparison between the two neural estimators reveals a tradeoff
across noise levels. The estimator trained with colored noise has a
$2.11$~dB advantage at $-10$~dB, while the estimator trained with
white noise performs better at high SNR.
The benefit of the modified denoiser is thus concentrated
at high input uncertainty, which motivates examining the receiver under
limited pilots and heavier access loads. The genie retains a substantial
advantage and has additional path information unavailable to either
learned estimator.
after:
At $0$~dB in Fig.~\ref{fig:cstmp-denoising}, the colored-trained
estimator reaches $-17.98$~dB NMSE versus $-2.98$~dB for the
Gaussian-prior estimator, demonstrating the value of structure beyond
average power. The learned estimators continue improving at high SNR,
whereas sparse recovery flattens, consistent with residual dictionary
and first-order offset approximation error. Colored training's
estimator gains $2.11$~dB over the white-trained estimator at $-10$~dB,
but the latter is better at high SNR. The benefit is therefore
concentrated at high input uncertainty. The genie remains better,
with additional path information unavailable to the learned estimators.

before:
Both trajectories initially increase in NMSE before entering a sustained
error-reduction phase. The approximate extrinsic updates do not enforce
a decrease in channel NMSE at each iteration. GP-CCD-MP-DRE approaches
its final accuracy by approximately $30$ iterations, while STMP continues
to improve over a longer interval. Their final NMSEs are $-13.85$ and
$-11.79$~dB, respectively. Thus, in this scene, the proposed receiver
reaches a lower error level earlier.
after:
Both trajectories initially increase in NMSE: approximate extrinsic
updates do not guarantee monotonic error reduction. GP-CCD-MP-DRE
approaches its final $-13.85$~dB by about $30$ iterations, while
STMP improves more slowly to $-11.79$~dB. This is a single-scene result.

before:
The NMSE curves exhibit two distinct trends. GP-CCD-MP-DRE and STMP
continue to benefit from increasing SNR, while the improvements of the
sparse-recovery baselines become smaller, widening the proposed
receiver's advantage over off-grid SBL. Together with the direct denoising
results, this separation
suggests that the retained sparse representations limit the benefit of
more accurate observations. In contrast, the gain over STMP narrows from
$1.87$~dB at $-4$~dB to $0.41$~dB at $6$~dB. Both receivers use learned
channel priors; the additional benefit of the proposed receiver is most
visible when the observations leave greater uncertainty about the channel.

Channel estimation and activity detection are coupled through
the joint moments in \eqref{eq:mixture}: the activity probability weights
the conditional channel estimate, and the resulting estimate is fed back
through MFLE. At $0$~dB, the proposed receiver reduces STMP's AER by about
$47\%$, mainly through fewer missed active devices. At $-4$~dB,
off-grid SBL has slightly lower AER but substantially higher NMSE:
correct activity decisions alone do not ensure accurate channel estimates.
after:
The learned receivers continue improving as SNR increases, while
sparse recovery improves less, consistent with the representation
constraints seen in direct denoising. The NMSE gain over STMP narrows
from $1.87$~dB at $-4$~dB to $0.41$~dB at $6$~dB.
At $0$~dB, GP-CCD-MP-DRE reduces STMP's AER by about $47\%$,
mainly through fewer misses. At $-4$~dB, off-grid SBL has slightly
lower AER but substantially higher NMSE, showing that accurate
activity decisions alone do not ensure accurate channel estimates.

before:
Increasing $Q$ provides more measurements of the same effective channel
at fixed per-frame pilot energy. The gain over STMP decreases from
$1.57$~dB at $Q=16$ to $0.51$~dB at $Q=48$, indicating that the proposed
receiver is most useful when the pilot observations provide weaker
constraints. This advantage translates into a lower pilot requirement:
on the evaluated grid, reaching $-14$~dB NMSE requires $24$ frames with
GP-CCD-MP-DRE and $32$ with STMP, a $25\%$ reduction. At $Q=48$, the two
methods attain the same AER while a channel-NMSE gap remains. Once most
activity errors have been removed, the accuracy of the estimated channel
coefficients still distinguishes the receivers.
after:
More pilot frames constrain the same channel at fixed per-frame
energy. The gain over STMP decreases from $1.57$~dB at $Q=16$
to $0.51$~dB at $Q=48$. Reaching $-14$~dB on the tested grid
requires $24$ frames with GP-CCD-MP-DRE versus $32$ with STMP,
a $25\%$ reduction. At $Q=48$, AER is equal but the channel-NMSE
gap remains.

before:
At fixed $p$, increasing $K$ enlarges both the set of candidate channels
and the expected active population. Each column of the observation model
still provides only $Q$ measurements, while the number of candidate
coefficients grows as $KN$. At the fixed aggregate SNR in \eqref{eq:snr},
the typical per-device SNR also decreases as more devices become active.
The resulting increase in estimation difficulty is visible in all six
curves, even though the nominal activity probability is unchanged.
GP-CCD-MP-DRE retains the lowest NMSE, with a widening advantage
over STMP. For a target NMSE of
$-10$~dB, the largest tested candidate populations meeting the target are
$80$ and $40$ for GP-CCD-MP-DRE and STMP, respectively. At $K=100$, the
proposed receiver also retains a $2.53$~dB advantage over off-grid SBL.
Thus, with the same number of pilot frames, the evaluated configuration accommodates
a larger candidate population at a prescribed estimation accuracy.
after:
Increasing $K$ at fixed $p$ raises both the candidate dimension
$KN$ and expected active population, while each observation column
still has $Q$ measurements. Fixed aggregate SNR also lowers typical
per-device SNR. NMSE consequently increases for all methods.
GP-CCD-MP-DRE remains best: at target $-10$~dB, the largest tested
candidate populations are $80$ versus $40$ for STMP; at $K=100$,
its advantage over off-grid SBL is $2.53$~dB.

before:
With $K$ fixed, this experiment keeps the candidate-channel dimension
unchanged and increases the fraction of active blocks. More channel
coefficients must be recovered from the same pilot and antenna resources,
with less activity sparsity available to constrain the solution. The
increasing NMSE is consistent with this reduced sparsity and the greater
load at fixed aggregate SNR. The proposed receiver
remains the most accurate, and its NMSE advantage over STMP grows from
$1.07$~dB at $p=0.05$ to $2.25$~dB at $p=0.25$. At the latter point,
off-grid SBL slightly surpasses STMP, while GP-CCD-MP-DRE still has a
$2.15$~dB advantage over off-grid SBL. Together with the device-count
experiment, these results show that the receiver retains its advantage
both as the candidate population expands and as simultaneous access
becomes denser within a fixed population.
after:
At fixed $K$, increasing activity raises the number of unknown active
coefficients without adding measurements, reducing activity sparsity.
GP-CCD-MP-DRE remains most accurate; its gain over STMP grows from
$1.07$~dB at $p=0.05$ to $2.25$~dB at $p=0.25$. At the latter
point, off-grid SBL slightly surpasses STMP but remains $2.15$~dB
behind GP-CCD-MP-DRE. Together with the device-count sweep, this
supports the proposed receiver under heavier access loads.

The preceding comparisons use profile D, which also supplies the
training channels. Figure~\ref{fig:cstmp-cross} examines whether the fixed
receivers retain their accuracy when the power-delay and fading profiles
change to A, B, and C, without retraining. Geometry and the receiver
settings remain fixed across profiles; each of the $24$ profile--SNR
conditions uses $500$ paired scenes. This comparison tests transfer of
the learned channel structure beyond the training profile.
after:
Figure~\ref{fig:cstmp-cross} transfers the receivers trained on
profile D to profiles A, B, and C without retraining. Geometry
and receiver settings remain fixed; each of the $24$ profile--SNR
conditions uses $500$ paired scenes.

before:
GP-CCD-MP-DRE remains substantially more accurate than the four
sparse-recovery baselines on every evaluated profile. Its advantage over
STMP, however, depends on the profile and SNR. At $0$~dB, the gains range
from $1.02$ to $1.60$~dB across the four profiles. The proposed receiver
remains better on D and C throughout the SNR range, but the curves cross
on A and B as noise decreases. On B they nearly coincide at $4$~dB;
at $6$~dB, STMP is better by $0.39$ and $0.58$~dB on A and B,
respectively. Thus, the fixed learned prior remains useful beyond the
training profile, while the high-SNR ordering of the two learned
receivers is profile-dependent.
after:
GP-CCD-MP-DRE outperforms the four sparse-recovery baselines on
every evaluated profile. Gains over STMP at $0$~dB range from
$1.02$ to $1.60$~dB. It remains better on D and C throughout
the SNR range, but the ordering changes on A and B: the B curves
nearly coincide at $4$~dB, and STMP is better by $0.39$ and
$0.58$~dB at $6$~dB on A and B, respectively. Thus the learned
prior transfers beyond profile D, with profile-dependent high-SNR performance.
